hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when you help someone, does part of you hope they’ll know it was you?
options: that’s human. this couple went the other way. listen.
then you’ll like these two. listen.
then this story might make you. listen.

steps.line: In Babylonia, a rabbi named Mar Ukba had a poor neighbor. Every day, he slipped four coins into the socket of the man’s door, where no one would see.
One day the poor man thought, “I’ll go and see who is doing this for me.” So he waited by the door.

steps.q: Mar Ukba and his wife arrive with the coins, and the door starts to open. What do they do?
o: Leave the coins and walk off slowly
steps.why: They ran. Being seen might make the man feel ashamed, so they hid.

steps.line: That day Mar Ukba was late from study, and his wife came with him. As the door opened, they ran and hid inside a baker’s oven, its fire just swept out.
The oven floor was still hot, and Mar Ukba’s feet were burning. His wife said, “Put your feet on mine.” And they waited, together, in the dark.

steps.q: Why would they rather sit in a hot oven than be seen?
o: They didn’t want everyone asking for coins
Their gift would no longer count
Being found out could shame the man
steps.why: The Talmud tells it to teach a line: better to throw yourself into a furnace than to shame someone in public. They nearly did.

steps.q: Mar Ukba’s feet burned, but his wife’s didn’t. The Talmud explains why. What does it say?
o: Her shoes were thicker than his
Her kind of giving was even greater
She had stepped where it was cooler
steps.why: She was at home, and handed the poor food ready to eat, while he gave coins they still had to spend. Her help arrived sooner.

steps.line: Centuries later, the great scholar Maimonides ranked tzedakah in eight levels, often pictured as a ladder. Giving in secret, so no one is ashamed, is near the top.
steps.label: a later teaching

steps.line: And the top rung, above all the rest? Helping someone so they won’t need help again: a loan, a partnership, a job.

steps.q: Mar Ukba knew who he was helping; the man didn’t know him. On Maimonides’ ladder, what kind of secret giving sits even higher?
o: When neither one knows the other
When the poor man knows, but no one else
When it’s given before he even asks
steps.why: Neither knows, like coins dropped into a community fund. Only one rung is higher: help that ends the need altogether.

steps.line: Today, many Jewish homes keep a small tzedakah box on the counter. Coins go in, often before Shabbat, a little at a time.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. tzedakah isn’t charity, a kindness you choose when you feel moved. it comes from tzedek, justice. part of what you have was never fully yours. it’s the poor person’s share.
that’s why the rabbis said even someone who lives on tzedakah should give a little. and maimonides noticed: one coin given a thousand times shapes you more than a thousand coins given once.

steps.q: Maimonides said a thousand coins given one at a time change you more than all at once. Why?
o: Small coins are easier to hide
The repeated act shapes the giver
It helps the poor person save
steps.why: Doing it again and again turns giving into who you are. That’s what the little box on the counter is for.

today.say: find a jar, a cup, or a box. today, put in one coin, before you feel like it. when it’s full, give it away, quietly. that’s tzedakah, one coin at a time.
options: one coin a day. mar ukba would smile.
good. that one coin is a rung on the ladder.

sources: Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 67b (Mar Ukba throws four zuz into his poor neighbor’s door socket every day; the poor man goes to see who it is; Mar Ukba, late from the house of study, comes with his wife; they flee into a furnace whose fire had been swept; his feet are scorched; she tells him to put his feet on hers; ‘better for a person to throw himself into a fiery furnace than to shame his fellow in public,’ Mar Zutra bar Toviah in the name of Rav; the lesson shortens this line and leaves out why her feet were spared)
Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Gifts to the Poor 10:7–14 (the eight levels; the highest is strengthening the poor person with a gift, loan, partnership or work)
Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 7b (even one who lives on tzedakah gives); Deuteronomy 16:20
Maimonides, Commentary on the Mishnah, Avot 3:15 (3:19 in some editions; a thousand coins given one at a time to a thousand people builds the trait more than one gift of a thousand)
check: ‘Often before Shabbat’ for the tzedakah box is a common home custom, not a law
